text: You can't wait for inspiration. You have to go after it with a club.
author: Jack London

text: A writer who waits for ideal conditions under which to work will die without putting a word on paper.
author: E.B. White

text: Amateurs sit and wait for inspiration, the rest of us just get up and go to work.
author: Stephen King

text: There is no greater agony than bearing an untold story inside you.
author: Maya Angelou
source: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings

text: The first draft is just you telling yourself the story.
author: Terry Pratchett

text: Don't get it right, get it written.
author: James Thurber

text: I write one page of masterpiece to ninety-one pages of shit. I try to put the shit in the wastebasket.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Start before you're ready.
author: Steven Pressfield

text: The scariest moment is always just before you start. After that, things can only get better.
author: Stephen King

text: We write to taste life twice, in the moment and in retrospect.
author: Anaïs Nin

text: A small daily task, if it be really daily, will beat the labours of a spasmodic Hercules.
author: Anthony Trollope

text: Inspiration is a guest that does not willingly visit the lazy.
author: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky

text: We must always work, and a self-respecting artist must not fold his hands on the pretext that he is not in the mood.
author: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky

text: Without craftsmanship, inspiration is a mere reed shaken in the wind.
author: Johannes Brahms

text: Write what disturbs you, what you fear, what you have not been willing to speak about. Be willing to be split open.
author: Natalie Goldberg

text: If you do not breathe through writing, if you do not cry out in writing, or sing in writing, then don't write, because our culture has no use for it.
author: Anaïs Nin

text: No tears in the writer, no tears in the reader. No surprise in the writer, no surprise in the reader.
author: Robert Frost

text: The most important things are the hardest to say, because words diminish them.
author: Stephen King

text: Write the book you want to read.
author: Toni Morrison

text: You must write every single day of your life. You must read dreadful dumb books and glorious books, and let them wrestle in beautiful fights inside your head.
author: Ray Bradbury
source: Zen in the Art of Writing

text: Stories may well be lies, but they are good lies that say true things.
author: Neil Gaiman

text: Be yourself. Above all, let who you are, what you are, what you believe shine through every sentence you write.
author: John Jakes

text: The art of writing is the art of discovering what you believe.
author: Gustave Flaubert

text: Fiction is the lie through which we tell the truth.
author: Albert Camus

text: All you have to do is write one true sentence. Write the truest sentence that you know.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Let me live, love, and say it well in good sentences.
author: Sylvia Plath
source: The Unabridged Journals of Sylvia Plath

text: A word after a word after a word is power.
author: Margaret Atwood

text: The true alchemists do not change lead into gold; they change the world into words.
author: William H. Gass

text: After nourishment, shelter and companionship, stories are the thing we need most in the world.
author: Philip Pullman

text: Writing is rewriting....To fall in love with the first draft to the point where one cannot change it is to greatly enhance the prospects of never publishing.
author: Richard North Patterson

text: I have rewritten — often several times — every word I have ever published. My pencils outlast their erasers.
author: Vladimir Nabokov

text: Easy reading is damn hard writing.
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne

text: Kill your darlings, kill your darlings, even when it breaks your egocentric little scribbler's heart, kill your darlings.
author: Stephen King

text: Prose is architecture, not interior decoration.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Clutter is the disease of American writing. We are a society strangling in unnecessary words.
author: William Zinsser

text: Omit needless words. Vigorous writing is concise.
author: William Strunk Jr.

text: This is how you do it: you sit down at the keyboard and you put one word after another until it's done. It's that easy, and that hard.
author: Neil Gaiman

text: Writing a book is a horrible, exhausting struggle, like a long bout with some painful illness....One would never undertake it if not driven by some demon one can neither resist nor understand.
author: George Orwell

text: There are three rules for writing a novel. Unfortunately, no one knows what they are.
author: W. Somerset Maugham

text: You simply sit down at the typewriter, open your veins, and bleed.
author: Red Smith

text: The difference between the right word and the almost right word is the difference between lightning and the lightning bug.
author: Mark Twain

text: Character is plot, plot is character.
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald

text: A character is what he does, not what he says.
author: Sol Stein

text: A story is not about what happens. It's about what it costs.
author: Robert McKee

text: The more specific you are, the more universal you become.
author: Ursula K. Le Guin

text: The human heart in conflict with itself is the only thing worth writing about.
author: William Faulkner

text: Every character should want something, even if it's only a glass of water.
author: Kurt Vonnegut

text: Words can be like X-rays if you use them properly — they'll go through anything. You read and you're pierced.
author: Aldous Huxley

text: When people talk, listen completely. Most people never listen.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Dialogue is a confrontation. It must always escalate.
author: Sol Stein

text: The best dialogue is one in which every sentence advances the story or reveals character — and the best sentences do both at once.
author: John Gardner

text: Don't tell me the moon is shining; show me the glint of light on broken glass.
author: Anton Chekhov

text: Tension is not suspense. Suspense is the reader caring what happens next. Tension is the reader afraid to find out.
author: Donald Maass

text: Everything in a story should happen for a reason, and every reason should matter.
author: John Gardner

text: The job of fiction is not to tell us how we should feel. The job of fiction is to make us feel.
author: Colum McCann

text: Make the reader feel, not think.
author: Sol Stein

text: A story is a living thing. You have to let it breathe.
author: Toni Morrison

text: Resistance is always lying and always full of shit.
author: Steven Pressfield

text: A professional writer is an amateur who didn't quit.
author: Richard Bach

text: You fail only if you stop writing.
author: Ray Bradbury

text: Writing is the only thing that when I do it, I don't feel I should be doing something else.
author: Gloria Steinem

text: I kept always two books in my pocket, one to read, one to write in.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

text: An artist must be free to choose what he does, certainly, but he must also never be afraid to do what he might choose.
author: Langston Hughes

text: Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

text: Without deviation from the norm, progress is not possible.
author: Frank Zappa

text: If you don't have time to read, you don't have the time — or the tools — to write. Simple as that.
author: Stephen King

text: Read, read, read. Read everything — trash, classics, good and bad, and see how they do it.
author: William Faulkner

text: The greatest part of a writer's time is spent in reading, in order to write.
author: Samuel Johnson

text: Delete filter words — 'she noticed,' 'she felt,' 'she saw.' Let the environment act....'The candle had gone out. Wax pooled on the saucer, still warm.'
author: Craft Principle

text: Climb the Specificity Ladder: 'a flower' ... 'a rose' ... 'a yellow climbing rose' ... 'a yellow climbing rose with aphids on the underside of every leaf.' Push every image at least one rung higher.
author: Craft Principle

text: Find an object in the scene and describe it using the vocabulary of the emotion....If you've written 'grief' or 'rage' as a noun in narrative prose, you've probably told instead of shown.
author: Craft Principle

text: Strip every sentence to its cleanest components. Read each sentence: remove every word that doesn't earn its place. If the sentence means the same thing without a word, that word is clutter.
author: William Zinsser

text: Adverbs doing a verb's job are clutter. 'Walked slowly' → shuffled. 'Said angrily' → snapped. Find the verb that already contains the modifier.
author: Craft Principle

text: A broken thing often carries more meaning than a whole one. The imperfect, asymmetrical image frequently lands harder than the polished one. Don't sand away productive roughness.
author: Craft Principle

text: A narrator shouldn't drift from musical imagery into botanical imagery into military imagery...unless the mix is deliberate. Metaphor consistency is voice consistency.
author: Craft Principle

text: If a passage makes you admire the writing instead of experiencing the story, it's overwritten. The best prose is invisible. You don't notice it — you notice what it describes.
author: Craft Principle

text: 'Said' is invisible to the reader's eye. Everything else — declared, announced, stated, interjected — draws attention to itself. Use 'said' and 'asked' freely. Reach for anything else sparingly.
author: Craft Principle

text: In high-stakes dialogue, no more than 10–30% of the emotional content should be spoken aloud. The rest lives beneath the surface — in what characters avoid...in the silences.
author: Craft Principle

text: Every line of dialogue is a thing a character does to another character. It can wound, seduce, deflect, test, comfort, or betray. If a line doesn't DO something to someone, consider cutting it.
author: Craft Principle

text: Cover the attribution tags and read only the dialogue. Can you tell who's speaking? If every character sounds interchangeable — same sentence length, same vocabulary — the voices need differentiation.
author: Craft Principle

text: The most powerful dialogue tool is silence. What isn't said, what's interrupted, what's deflected — these carry more weight than any spoken line. Ask: what are both characters refusing to say?
author: Craft Principle

text: Syntax is sheet music for the diaphragm. Short sentences force quick, shallow breaths. Long, subordinate-clause-heavy sentences slow the reader's breathing. Make the rhythm match the emotion.
author: Craft Principle

text: Ask the 'And then what?' test at the end of every paragraph....If the paragraph resolves its own energy, the reader can close the book there — dangerous mid-scene.
author: Craft Principle

text: Every scene must change something — a relationship, a belief, the stakes....If characters exit the same way they entered, the scene is stalling. Give every scene a 'before' and 'after.'
author: Craft Principle

text: Vary scene length deliberately. Follow a long, immersive scene with a short, compressed one....Metronomic scene lengths flatten the reader's sense of time.
author: Craft Principle

text: Tension is not the same as action. A character sitting alone in a room can be more tense than a swordfight — if the reader is waiting....Seed dramatic irony into quiet scenes.
author: Donald Maass

text: Expand the moments that change everything. Compress the moments that maintain the status quo. A turning point summarized in a sentence is a turning point the reader can't feel.
author: Craft Principle

text: A character's want (what they're chasing) and their need (what they actually require) should be in conflict. The tension between want and need is where character arcs live.
author: Craft Principle

text: Your character's flaw is not a handicap — it's the engine. What your protagonist cannot yet do or be is what the story is about teaching them. Remove the flaw and you remove the arc.
author: Craft Principle

text: What a character notices reveals who they are....Ask: would anyone notice this, or only this specific person? If anyone would notice it, find a stranger, more specific detail.
author: Craft Principle
source: Language & Style / The 'Only This Character' Test

text: Show don't tell isn't an absolute — it's a calibration. Tell summary; show the moments that change everything. Reserve real-time scene for the...moments the reader needs to inhabit.
author: Ursula K. Le Guin

text: Emotion lands in the body, not the label. Don't write 'she was devastated.' Write what devastation does: the mug left in the sink...the radio turned on, then off.
author: Craft Principle

text: Voice is not style. Style is how sentences are arranged. Voice is the consciousness behind the sentences — what this particular mind considers worth noticing, worth saying, worth leaving out.
author: Craft Principle

text: Ask of every edit: would THIS narrator think this thought in THIS way? The writer's job is not to improve the prose in the abstract. It's to make the prose more fully itself.
author: Craft Principle
